key_terms.meaning: Process that starts a request for a service.
Process that waits for requests and provides a service.
Architecture where each peer can act as both client and server.
Client talks directly to one server tier, often a database server.
Client, application server and data server are separate tiers.
Server keeps no per-client session information between requests.
Server remembers session or connection context across requests.
One endpoint of a conversation, named by IP address and port number.
Socket that provides a reliable byte stream after connect and accept.
Socket that sends and receives independent datagrams without a connection.
Client-side process that sends DNS queries and follows referrals.
DNS query where the contacted server must return the final answer.
Stateless request-reply protocol carried on a TCP connection.
FTP TCP connection that carries commands for the whole session.
FTP TCP connection that carries file contents; opened per transfer.
FTP mode where the client opens the data connection to the server.
Push protocol that sends mail from client to server and server to server.
Extension that labels mail body parts with type and encoding.
Same secret key encrypts and decrypts data.
Firewall that tracks connection state and allows return traffic.

takeaways: The chosen application architecture decides where state, control and scaling limits live.
A socket is one IP address plus one port; TCP gives a byte stream and UDP gives datagrams.
DNS resolves names through a hierarchy of servers and uses caching to cut repeated round trips.
HTTP is a short, stateless request-reply protocol; cookies add remembered state.
FTP keeps commands on a control connection and sends each file on a separate data connection.
Email is pushed by SMTP to the receiver's mail server and pulled out by POP3 or IMAP.
Network security aims at confidentiality, integrity and authentication.
Firewalls range from stateless filters to stateful firewalls and application proxies, with a DMZ for public servers.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for protocol flows, socket calls, message formats and a clear mapping from attacks to security controls.

bank.q: Compare client-server and peer-to-peer application architectures. Explain two-tier and three-tier designs, the role of a central directory, and when a server is stateless or stateful.
outline: client asks, server provides; peer can be both
two-tier: client to server/database; three-tier: client, application server, data server
central directory helps peers find each other
stateless vs stateful affects cookies, sessions and scaling

bank.q: Explain a socket as an IP address plus port. Describe the main calls for a TCP server and client, and how UDP socket calls differ.
outline: socket endpoint, port identifies process
TCP calls: socket, bind, listen, accept, connect, read/write, close
UDP calls: socket, sendto, recvfrom; no connection setup
blocking and message boundaries differ

bank.q: Describe the DNS name space and the steps of name-to-address resolution. Distinguish recursive and iterative queries and explain caching.
outline: tree: root, top-level domains, authoritative servers
resolver asks root, then TLD, then authoritative server
recursive server does work; iterative server returns referral
cache with TTL reduces lookups

bank.q: Explain HTTP as a request-reply protocol over TCP. Include request line, headers, methods, status codes, statelessness and cookies.
outline: TCP connection carries readable request and reply
method, path, version; headers; body
status code classes 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx
HTTP keeps no state; cookies and server sessions add state

bank.q: Explain FTP control and data connections. Compare active and passive modes and give one reason each is used.
outline: control connection stays open for commands
data connection opened per file transfer
active: server connects back to client
passive: client connects to server; helps with NAT and firewalls

bank.q: Explain how email moves from sender to receiver using SMTP, POP3 and IMAP. Show the role of MIME and the main SMTP commands.
outline: user agent to mail server; SMTP between servers
commands: EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA, QUIT
MIME carries non-text content
POP3 downloads; IMAP keeps server state and folders

bank.q: Trace what happens when a user types a URL and presses Enter, from DNS lookup through TCP connection to HTTP response. Where can caching occur?
outline: parse URL; DNS cache and resolver lookup
TCP connect to server IP and port 80 or 443
send HTTP request; server returns status, headers, body
caches at browser, DNS resolver and HTTP proxy or CDN

bank.q: Write pseudocode for a TCP echo server and client. Explain why the receiver still needs message framing even though TCP is reliable.
outline: server: socket, bind, listen, accept, read, write
client: socket, connect, write, read
TCP is a byte stream, not message records
use length prefix or delimiter to find message ends

bank.q: An FTP client is behind a NAT. Explain why passive mode often works better than active mode, using control and data connections.
outline: control connection is client to server
active mode: server opens data connection to client port
NAT may block inbound connection to client
passive mode: client opens data connection to server data port

bank.q: Describe the SMTP dialogue for sending one message from alice@a.example to bob@b.example, then how Bob retrieves it with IMAP. List commands in order.
outline: EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA, message, period, QUIT
server queues and delivers to bob's mail server
IMAP login, select mailbox, fetch message
MIME headers identify content type

bank.q: Map confidentiality, integrity and authentication to eavesdropping, tampering, masquerading and replay. Which tool serves each goal?
outline: eavesdropping countered by encryption
tampering countered by integrity check or MAC
masquerading countered by authentication and certificates
replay countered by nonces, timestamps or sequence numbers

bank.q: Compare stateless packet filter, stateful firewall and application proxy. Where does a DMZ fit and what does each control cost?
outline: packet filter uses header fields only; fast but limited
stateful firewall tracks connections; better return traffic control
proxy inspects application data; slower and more complex
DMZ holds public servers between internet and internal network

bank.q: HTTP is stateless. Analyse how cookies and server-side sessions add state, and the privacy and scaling tradeoffs.
outline: cookie stores identifier at client
session state stored at server or in token
scaling needs shared session store
privacy risks from tracking and stolen cookies

bank.q: Compare TCP and UDP for HTTP, DNS, live video and a chat app. Justify each choice with reliability, delay and connection overhead.
outline: HTTP uses TCP for reliable ordered bytes
DNS uses UDP for short queries and TCP for large or zone transfer
live video may use UDP and tolerate loss
chat needs reliability; TCP or reliable UDP layer

glossary.def: Separate logical layers in an application architecture, such as client, application server and data server.
Shared index that peers use to find other peers or resources.
Peer-to-peer network with no central index or control point.
Public FTP service that accepts a generic anonymous login.
FTP transfer type for ASCII text with end-of-line conversion.
FTP transfer type for raw binary with no line conversion.
FTP mode where the server opens the data connection back to the client.
SMTP command that starts the message body and ends with a line containing only a period.
SMTP command that opens a session and asks for supported extensions.
SMTP command that names the sender.
SMTP command that names one recipient.
Mail access protocol that keeps messages on the server and supports folders and synchronised state.
Simple mail access protocol that usually downloads messages to one client.
Server-side storage area for a user's email.
Host that stores mailboxes and runs SMTP and mail access protocols.
Messages waiting for SMTP delivery attempts.
Mail program the user reads and composes messages with.
Network segment between the internet and internal network that holds public-facing servers.
Passive reading of messages on the network.
Pretending to be another party or host.
Re-sending a valid captured message later.
Unauthorised change of data in transit.
Firewall that decides each packet alone from header fields.
Firewall that terminates and inspects application protocol sessions.
Attack that makes a service unavailable by exhausting resources.
Encryption with public and private keys; the public key encrypts and the private key decrypts.
